concepts.definition: A small function that does a single job for the robot: it says whether it is active and what it suggests for the wheels.
concepts.example: The `KAC` (escape) behaviour becomes active when the front distance drops below 25 cm and suggests turning left on the spot.
concepts.pitfall: Driving the motor directly inside the behaviour: two behaviours write to the motor at the same time and the result becomes unpredictable.

concepts.definition: A behaviour's answer to the arbiter: active or not, left speed, right speed.
concepts.example: Oneri o = {true, -140, 140}; that is, I am active, left wheel backwards, right wheel forwards.
concepts.pitfall: Writing aktif = true for all behaviours: the arbiter always picks the first one, and the others never run again.

concepts.definition: Code that goes through the suggestions in priority order, picks the first active one and drives the motors only with it.
concepts.example: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { if (oneri[i].aktif) { secilen = i; break; } }
concepts.pitfall: Mixing up the order: if you put the default behaviour first, the others are never chosen.

concepts.definition: The order between behaviours. The behaviour that comes first in the order overrides the one behind it.
concepts.example: `KAC` comes before `CIZGI` (line); that is why it does not hit the wall even while the line is visible.
concepts.pitfall: Setting priorities without thinking: on a fire robot, if 'escape from obstacles' is at the top, the robot may never get close to the smoke.

concepts.definition: Using different thresholds for starting and ending a behaviour.
concepts.example: `KAC` starts at 25 cm and ends when it goes past 60 cm.
concepts.pitfall: Using a single threshold: around the threshold the robot keeps switching back and forth between `KAC` and `DOLAS` (wander).

quiz.prompt: The arbiter picks the first active behaviour in priority order (`KAC`, `CIZGI`, `DOLAS`). The robot is on the line and 20 cm from the wall, so both `KAC` and `CIZGI` are active. Which one drives the motors?
options: `KAC`, because it comes first in the order and is the first active one
quiz.explanation: The arbiter loop sees `KAC` (number 0), and because it is active it stops with break; it never looks at `CIZGI`. No average is taken and the suggestions are not mixed. `DOLAS` is always active but comes last; it is only chosen when the others are not active.

At i = 0, aktif[0] is false, so it carries on. At i = 1, aktif[1] is true: secilen becomes 1 and break ends the loop. It does not print 2; that is only the starting value, and the loop overwrites it. 3 is not the number of any behaviour.

quiz.prompt: `KAC` starts below 25 cm and ends when it goes above 60 cm. The measurements, in order: 30, 24, 40, 58, 61, 50 cm. In how many measurements is `KAC` active?
quiz.explanation: 30 cm: it has not started yet. 24 cm: it starts (1). 40 cm: below 60, it carries on (2). 58 cm: still below 60, it carries on (3). 61 cm: it ends. 50 cm: it is not below 25, so it does not start again. Total 3. With a single threshold it would have been active only at 24 cm.

options: The Oneri struct cannot contain a bool
The behaviour drives the motor itself; even if the arbiter picks another behaviour, this line writes to the motors
The return o; line is unnecessary
quiz.explanation: Behaviours should only return a suggestion; the arbiter drives the motor. Here, as soon as kac() is called (before the arbiter has chosen), it writes to the motors. The threshold value is deliberately 25. A bool field is allowed in structs. return o; is required so the arbiter gets the suggestion.

quiz.prompt: The HC-SR04 echo time was measured as 1160 µs. The code uses distance = time / 58.0. What is the front distance in cm?
quiz.explanation: 1160 / 58 = 20 cm. Because the sound goes there and back, the time covers both ways; 58 µs/cm is a factor that takes this into account. Because the `KAC` threshold is 25 cm, `KAC` takes over at this measurement.
